## 실무에서의 CLV 활용 {#sec-clv-production}

학술적 CLV와 실무적 LTV는 종종 괴리를 보인다. 프로덕션 환경에서 공식은 비즈니스 모델과 가용 데이터에 의해 좌우되며, 학술 문헌보다 훨씬 단순한 도구로 계산되는 경우가 많아 아래에서 설명하는 실무적 함정들이 반복적으로 발생한다.

### 실무에서 실제로 사용되는 공식들 {#sec-clv-formulas}

SaaS 및 구독 비즈니스에서 가장 널리 사용되는 LTV 공식은 다음과 같다:

$$
\text{LTV} \;=\; \frac{\text{ARPA} \times \text{매출총이익률(\%)}}{\text{이탈률(churn rate)}},
$$ {#eq-clv-naive}

여기서 ARPA는 계정당 평균 매출(Average Revenue Per Account)이고 $1/\text{churn}$은 암묵적인 기대 수명이다. [@eq-clv-naive]는 $r=0$이고 일정한 유지율 $\rho = 1 - \text{churn}$을 가정한 [@eq-clv-geometric]과 동일하다. 대시보드의 두 수치만으로 계산할 수 있다는 장점이 있지만 네 가지 위험이 있다: (1) 이탈률의 불변성을 가정하지만 실제 유지율 곡선은 기간이 지남에 따라 평탄해지므로(sBG 모형이 설명하는 선별 효과) 잔존 고객의 가치를 *과소평가*한다. (2) 이탈률로 나누기 때문에 이탈률이 0에 가까워질수록 가치가 폭발한다. (3) 할인을 무시한다. (4) 확장 매출을 무시하여 순매출 유지율(NRR)이 100%를 초과하는 기업의 가치를 심각하게 과소평가한다.

올바른 공식은 [@eq-clv-from-survivor]에 제시된 코호트 기반 할인 모형이다.

고객 수준 상위에는 성장 모델의 건전성을 평가하는 이사회 수준의 *단위 경제학 지표*가 존재한다:
- **CAC(고객 획득 비용)**: 해당 기간의 총 영업·마케팅 지출을 획득된 신규 고객 수로 나눈 값.
- **LTV:CAC 비율**: 획득 고객 가치 대 획득 비용 비율. 벤처 업계에서는 일반적으로 $\ge 3:1$을 건전한 수준으로, $1:1$ 미만은 손실로, $5:1$ 초과는 성장에 대한 *과소* 투자 신호로 간주한다.
- **CAC 회수 기간(payback period)**: CAC를 고객당 월간 마진으로 나눈 개월 수. SaaS에서는 12개월 미만이 일반적 목표다.

### SaaS 유지 지표: 로고 대 달러, 총 대 순 유지율 {#sec-clv-saas-metrics}

구독 비즈니스는 두 가지 축을 따라 코호트 수준의 유지율을 보고한다. 첫째는 *로고(고객 수)* 유지율 대 *달러(매출)* 유지율이다: 잔존 계정이 확장되면 많은 소규모 고객(로고)을 잃더라도 달러 매출은 성장할 수 있다. 둘째는 *총(gross)* 대 *순(net)* 유지율이다. 총 매출 유지율(GRR)은 순수한 이탈 및 축소 손실만을 측정하며 최대 100%로 제한된다:

$$
\text{GRR} \;=\; \frac{\text{기초 MRR} - \text{이탈} - \text{축소}}{\text{기초 MRR}},
$$ {#eq-grr}

순 매출 유지율(NRR, 또는 순 달러 유지율)은 확장(업셀, 계정 확장, 크로스셀)을 다시 더하며 100%를 초과할 수 있다:

$$
\text{NRR} \;=\; \frac{\text{기초 MRR} - \text{이탈} - \text{축소} + \text{확장}}{\text{기초 MRR}},
$$ {#eq-nrr}

NRR이 100%를 초과한다는 것은 *신규 고객 유치 없이도* 기존 고객 기반만으로 매출이 성장함을 의미하므로 구독 소프트웨어에서 가장 주목받는 지표다.

### 기업 유형별 플레이북 {#sec-clv-playbook}

[@tbl-clv-playbook]은 산업별 비즈니스 모델에 따른 CLV 계산 방식을 보여준다.

| 기업 유형 | 계약 여부 | 데이터 | 프로덕션 CLV 계산 방식 | 전형적 도구 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SaaS / B2B 구독 | 계약적 | 결제/CRM, 코호트별 MRR | 코호트 유지 곡선 + NRR/GRR; LTV:CAC 및 회수 기간; 로고 이탈에 대한 sBG 또는 생존 모형 | dbt/SQL; `lifelines`; 스프레드시트 |
| 전자상거래 / D2C | 비계약적 | 주문 로그 (ID, 일자, 금액) | BTYD: BG/NBD(거래) + Gamma-Gamma(지출)로 pLTV 산출, 세분화 및 광고 입찰 연동 | R `CLVTools`/`BTYD`; Python `lifetimes`; 2단계 ML |
| 소매 / 소비재(CPG) | 비계약적 | 멤버십 패널, 장바구니 | 패널/멤버십 BTYD 또는 구조적 CLV [@sunder2016measuring]; 지갑 점유율; 카테고리 CLV | 패널 계량경제학; 위계적 베이즈; DW |
| 통신 / 보험 / 금융 | 계약적 | 가입기간, 이용량, 청구 | 생존/이탈 모형(Cox, XGBoost)으로 유지 곡선 및 할인 CLV 도출; 방어 타깃팅을 위한 업리프트 | `survival`/`lifelines`; XGBoost; SAS |
| 모바일 게임 / 앱 | 비계약, 프리미엄 | 이벤트 로그 | 초기 플레이 데이터 기반 ML pLTV; 고액 결제자(whale) 식별; ZILN 또는 2단계 모형; UA 입찰 | TensorFlow; 그래디언트 부스팅; 피처 스토어 |
| 미디어 / 스트리밍 | 구독 + 광고 혼합 | 시청 이력 + 구독 상태 | 콘텐츠 인게이지먼트 공변량을 포함한 코호트 유지율; 구독 생존 분석; 광고 지원 티어 ARPU 혼합 | DW 코호트; 생존 분석; ML |

: 기업 유형별 고객 평생 가치 계산 방식. {#tbl-clv-playbook}

### 프로덕션 스택과 반복되는 함정 {#sec-clv-pitfalls}

1. *단순 불변 이탈률 공식*([@eq-clv-naive]): LTV를 왜곡하고 이탈률이 0에 가까울 때 발산함.
2. *생존자 편향(Survivorship bias)*: 현재까지 생존한 고객만을 대상으로 유지 곡선을 적합하면 유지율이 과대평가됨. 중도절단 및 이탈 고객이 포함되어야 함.
3. *미래 정보 누수(Target leakage)*: 예측 대상 기간의 정보를 사용하여 특징(feature)을 생성하면 오프라인 정확도는 부풀려지고 프로덕션에서는 붕괴함.
4. *할인 무시*: 수개년 LTV를 할인하지 않으면 현재 가치가 과대평가됨.
5. *코호트 혼합(Cohort blending)*: 채널별·시기별 획득 코호트를 혼합하면 유료 채널 고객이 유기적 유입 고객보다 빠르게 이탈한다는 사실을 가리게 됨.
6. *예측된 CLV/이탈 확률을 타깃팅 정책으로 오인*: 이탈 확률의 수준은 고객의 *설득 가능성(persuadability)*과 다름([@sec-clv-causal] 참조).
7. *짧은 관찰 창의 무리한 외삽*([@fig-retention-projected] 참조).
8. *내생적 마케팅 지출*: 관찰된 유지율은 부분적으로 타깃 마케팅 지출에 대한 반응이므로 단순 상관관계는 인과적 수익률이 아님.

## 유지, 생존 및 Shifted-Beta-Geometric (sBG) 모형 {#sec-clv-sbg}

*계약적* 환경에서 관심 대상은 생존 함수 $S(t) = \Pr(\text{시점 } t \text{까지 활성 유지})$이다. 일정한 유지율 $\rho$를 가정한 $S(t)=\rho^t$는 실제 관찰되는 유지율 곡선이 기간이 지남에 따라 상승하는 현상을 설명하지 못한다. 오래 유지된 고객은 본질적으로 충성도가 높은 고객들이며, 이탈 성향이 높은 고객은 이미 떠났기 때문이다. 이는 개인이 더 충성스러워져서가 아니라 생존 집단이 충성도 높은 집단으로 선별되는 순수한 *선별(sorting/heterogeneity)* 효과다.

shifted-beta-geometric (sBG) 모형은 이러한 직관을 공식화한다 [@faderhardie2007sbg]. 각 고객은 고정되었지만 미관찰된 기간별 이탈 확률 $\theta$를 가진다. $\theta$가 주어졌을 때 이탈 시점은 기하 분포를 따른다:

$$
P(T = t \mid \theta) = \theta\,(1-\theta)^{\,t-1}, \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots
$$ {#eq-sbg-geometric}

고객 간의 이질성은 베타 사전분포 $\theta \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$로 포착된다. 이를 적분하면 $(\alpha,\beta)$에만 의존하는 집계 이탈 및 생존 함수가 도출된다:

$$
P(T = t) = \frac{B(\alpha+1,\;\beta+t-1)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}, \qquad
S(t) = \frac{B(\alpha,\;\beta+t)}{B(\alpha,\beta)} .
$$ {#eq-sbg-survivor}

이는 전방 점화식 $P(1)=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$, $P(t)=P(t-1)\,(\beta+t-2)/(\alpha+\beta+t-1)$, $S(t)=S(t-1)-P(t)$를 만족한다.

**추정.** 기간 $\tau$까지 관찰된 코호트 데이터에 대해 로그우도 함수는 다음과 같다:

$$
\ell(\alpha,\beta) = \sum_{t=1}^{\tau} d_t \,\log P(T=t)
   \;+\; n_{\tau}\,\log S(\tau),
$$ {#eq-sbg-loglik}

여기서 $d_t$는 기간 $t$의 이탈자 수, $n_{\tau}$는 $\tau$ 시점의 잔존 고객 수(우측 중도절단 기여분)이다.

아래 예제는 8개월간 관찰된 4개 구독 코호트 데이터를 바탕으로 sBG 모형을 적합하고 시각화한다.

```{r clv-setup}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-retention-observed
#| fig-cap: "4개 구독 코호트의 월별 관찰 유지율 곡선. 모두 하락하지만 감소 속도와 곡률이 상이함."
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(13)

df_ret <- tibble(
  month_lt = 0:7,
  case01 = c(1, .531, .452, .423, .394, .375, .356, .346),
  case02 = c(1, .869, .743, .653, .593, .551, .517, .491),
  case03 = c(1, .677, .562, .486, .412, .359, .332, .310),
  case04 = c(1, .631, .468, .382, .326, .289, .262, .241)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-month_lt, names_to = "example", values_to = "retention_rate")

ggplot(df_ret, aes(month_lt, retention_rate, colour = example)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ example) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#4e79a7", "#f28e2b", "#e15759", "#76b7b2")) +
  labs(x = "가입 후 경과 월수", y = "유지율") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

sBG 이탈, 생존 및 음의 로그우도 함수를 구현하고 최적화한다.

```{r sbg-functions}
# Beta-geometric 혼합에 따른 집계 이탈 확률 P(T = t) 전방 점화식 구현
churn_bg <- Vectorize(function(alpha, beta, period) {
  p <- alpha / (alpha + beta)
  if (period > 1)
    p <- churn_bg(alpha, beta, period - 1) *
         (beta + period - 2) / (alpha + beta + period - 1)
  p
}, vectorize.args = "period")

# 생존 함수 S(t) = S(t-1) - P(t), S(1) = 1 - P(1)
survival_bg <- Vectorize(function(alpha, beta, period) {
  s <- 1 - churn_bg(alpha, beta, 1)
  if (period > 1)
    s <- survival_bg(alpha, beta, period - 1) - churn_bg(alpha, beta, period)
  s
}, vectorize.args = "period")

# 음의 로그우도 함수 (수식 @eq-sbg-loglik)
neg_loglik <- function(par, active, lost) {
  alpha <- par[1]; beta <- par[2]
  tau <- length(active)
  -( sum(lost * log(churn_bg(alpha, beta, 1:tau))) +
       active[tau] * log(survival_bg(alpha, beta, tau)) )
}

df_ret <- df_ret |>
  group_by(example) |>
  mutate(active = 1000 * retention_rate,
         lost   = replace_na(lag(active) - active, 0)) |>
  ungroup()
```

초기 $i$개월만으로 모형을 적합하여 투영한 곡선들이 데이터가 누적됨에 따라 어떻게 안정화되는지 시각화한다.

```{r sbg-projections}
#| label: fig-retention-projected
#| fig-cap: "실제 관찰 유지율(굵은 선)과 초기 i개월 데이터만으로 적합한 sBG 투영 곡선(i = 1..7, 흐린 선). 관찰 기간이 길어질수록 투영치가 실제 곡선으로 수렴함."
project_cohort <- function(d) {
  map_dfr(1:7, function(i) {
    fit <- d |> filter(month_lt >= 1, month_lt <= i)
    opt <- optim(c(1, 1), neg_loglik,
                 active = fit$active, lost = fit$lost)
    tibble(month_lt   = 0:7,
           fact_months = i,
           retention_pred = round(
             c(1, survival_bg(opt$par[1], opt$par[2], 1:7)), 3))
  })
}

ret_preds <- df_ret |>
  group_by(example) |>
  group_modify(~ project_cohort(.x)) |>
  ungroup()

df_plot <- df_ret |>
  select(month_lt, example, retention_rate) |>
  left_join(ret_preds, by = c("month_lt", "example"))

ggplot(df_plot, aes(month_lt, retention_rate, colour = example)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = retention_pred, group = fact_months), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ example) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#4e79a7", "#f28e2b", "#e15759", "#76b7b2")) +
  labs(x = "가입 후 경과 월수", y = "유지율") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

### 유지율에서 가치로 {#sec-clv-retention-to-value}

적합된 생존 함수로부터 $N$기간에 걸친 기대 할인 가치는 다음과 같이 계산된다:

$$
\widehat{\text{CLV}} \;=\; m \sum_{t=0}^{N} \frac{\widehat{S}(t)}{(1+r)^{\,t}}.
$$ {#eq-clv-from-survivor}

2개월의 이력만을 바탕으로 코호트 3의 24개월 누적 LTV를 계산한다.

```{r clv-forecast}
fit3 <- df_ret |> filter(example == "case03", month_lt >= 1, month_lt <= 2)
opt3 <- optim(c(1, 1), neg_loglik, active = fit3$active, lost = fit3$lost)

projected <- tibble(
  month_lt       = 3:24,
  retention_pred = round(survival_bg(opt3$par[1], opt3$par[2], 3:24), 3))

ltv3 <- df_ret |>
  filter(example == "case03", month_lt <= 2) |>
  select(month_lt, retention_rate) |>
  bind_rows(projected) |>
  mutate(retention = coalesce(retention_rate, retention_pred),
         ltv_monthly = retention * 1,          # 1달러 구독료
         ltv_cum     = round(cumsum(ltv_monthly), 2))

tail(ltv3, 3)
cat("코호트 3의 24개월 평균 예상 LTV: $", tail(ltv3$ltv_cum, 1), "\n", sep = "")
```

## 고객 기반 분석을 위한 확률론적 모형 {#sec-clv-btyd}

*비계약적* 환경에서 Buy-Till-You-Die (BTYD) 모형군은 활성 상태에서의 *구매* 과정과 미관찰 시점에 관계를 종료하는 *이탈* 과정을 상정하고, 최근성(Recency)과 빈도(Frequency)로부터 미래 거래 및 가치를 도출한다.

### Pareto/NBD와 BG/NBD {#sec-clv-pnbd}

*Pareto/NBD* [@paretonbd1987]는 포아송 구매율 $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(r,\alpha)$와 지수 이탈률 $\mu \sim \text{Gamma}(s,\beta)$를 결합한다. *BG/NBD* [@fader2005bgnbd]는 계산상 복잡한 파레토 이탈 과정을 베타-기하 과정으로 대체하여 추정을 용이하게 만들었다. *Gamma-Gamma* 모형 [@fader2005rfmclv]은 지출액 차원을 모델링한다.

### 비계약적 파이프라인 실습 {#sec-clv-btyd-code}

Pareto/NBD 데이터 생성 과정으로부터 거래 로그를 시뮬레이션하고 `CLVTools` 및 `BTYD` 패키지로 적합한다.

```{r btyd-sim}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(42)

n_cust  <- 1500
T_total <- 78                       # 78주간 관찰

lambda    <- rgamma(n_cust, shape = 0.55, rate = 10)  # 주간 구매율
mu        <- rgamma(n_cust, shape = 0.40, rate = 30)  # 이탈률
cust_mean <- rgamma(n_cust, shape = 4,   rate = 0.08) # 잠재 평균 지출 (~$50)

sim_one <- function(i) {
  end <- min(rexp(1, mu[i]), T_total)
  ts <- 0; t <- 0
  repeat {
    t <- t + rexp(1, lambda[i])
    if (t > end) break
    ts <- c(ts, t)
  }
  tibble(cust = i, t = ts)
}

log_df <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_cust), sim_one) |>
  mutate(amount = rgamma(n(), shape = 6, rate = 6 / cust_mean[cust]),
         date   = as.Date("2020-01-01") + round(t * 7)) |>
  transmute(cust_id = paste0("C", cust), date, amount = round(amount, 2))

cat("행 수:", nrow(log_df),
    " 고객 수:", n_distinct(log_df$cust_id),
    " 기간:", as.character(min(log_df$date)), "~",
    as.character(max(log_df$date)), "\n")
```

`CLVTools`를 활용하여 52주 전방 할인 CLV를 예측한다.

```{r btyd-clvtools}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(CLVTools)

clv_dat <- clvdata(log_df, date.format = "ymd", time.unit = "week",
                   name.id = "cust_id", name.date = "date", name.price = "amount")

fit_pnbd <- pnbd(clv_dat, verbose = FALSE)
fit_gg   <- gg(clv_dat,   verbose = FALSE)

round(coef(fit_pnbd), 3)

pred <- predict(fit_pnbd, predict.spending = fit_gg,
                prediction.end = 52,
                continuous.discount.factor = 0.0029,  # 연간 약 15%
                verbose = FALSE) |>
  as.data.frame()

pred |>
  transmute(Id, PAlive = round(PAlive, 3), CET = round(CET, 2),
            지출예측 = round(predicted.mean.spending, 1),
            DERT  = round(DERT, 2),
            pLTV  = round(predicted.CLV, 2)) |>
  head(6)

cat("평균 예측 1년 CLV: $", round(mean(pred$predicted.CLV), 2), "\n", sep = "")
```

`BTYD` 패키지로 재추정하여 일관성을 교차 검증한다.

```{r btyd-crosscheck}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: hide
library(BTYD)

end_cal <- as.Date("2020-01-01") + 39 * 7

elog <- log_df |>
  transmute(cust = cust_id, date = as.Date(date), sales = amount) |>
  as.data.frame()

elog_m  <- dc.MergeTransactionsOnSameDate(elog)
cbs_cbt <- dc.ElogToCbsCbt(elog_m, per = "week", T.cal = end_cal)
cal_cbs <- cbs_cbt$cal$cbs

params_bg <- bgnbd.EstimateParameters(cal_cbs)
cet_btyd  <- bgnbd.ConditionalExpectedTransactions(
  params_bg, T.star = 13,
  x = cal_cbs[, "x"], t.x = cal_cbs[, "t.x"], T.cal = cal_cbs[, "T.cal"])
```

```{r btyd-crosscheck-out}
cat("BTYD BG/NBD 모수 (r, alpha, a, b):", round(params_bg, 3), "\n")
cat("13주 기대 거래 수 평균 (BTYD BG/NBD):",
    round(mean(cet_btyd), 3), "\n")
```

[@fig-clv-palive]는 최근성과 빈도에 따른 고객 활성 확률 P(alive) 히트맵을 보여준다.

```{r palive-heatmap}
#| label: fig-clv-palive
#| fig-cap: "적합된 BG/NBD 모형 하에서 최근성-빈도 격자에 따른 고객 활성 확률 P(alive). 구매 빈도가 높고 최근 방문이 가까울수록 생존 확률이 1에 가깝고, 적은 구매 후 침묵이 길어지면 이탈 확률이 높아짐."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
grid <- expand_grid(x = 0:10, t.x = seq(0, 39, by = 3)) |>
  mutate(palive = bgnbd.PAlive(params_bg, x = x, t.x = t.x, T.cal = 39))

ggplot(grid, aes(t.x, x, fill = palive)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "P(생존)", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "최근성: 마지막 구매 시점 (경과 주수)",
       y = "빈도: 반복 구매 횟수") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 계량경제학 및 위계적 베이즈 CLV {#sec-clv-econometric}

계량경제학적 전통은 공변량을 결합하여 구성요소들을 개별 모델링한다. @abe2009 는 Pareto/NBD를 위계적 베이즈 모형으로 재구성하여 공변량이 구매율과 이탈률을 이동시킬 수 있도록 확장했다 [@venkatesankumar2004; @reinartzkumar2003; @schweidel2008bivariate; @donkers2007clv].

마르코프 체인 정식화 [@pfeifercarraway2000]에서 상태별 평생 가치 벡터 $\mathbf{V}$는 전이행렬 $P$, 기간 보상 벡터 $\mathbf{r}$, 할인인자 $\gamma = 1/(1+r)$에 대해 다음 선형 시스템을 푼다:

$$
\mathbf{V} \;=\; (\mathbf{I} - \gamma P)^{-1}\,\mathbf{r}.
$$ {#eq-clv-markov}

[@fig-clv-states]와 [@tbl-clv-markov]는 3상태 고객 마이그레이션 모형의 구조와 가치를 보여준다.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-clv-states
%%| fig-cap: "마르코프 체인 CLV의 3상태 고객 마이그레이션 프로세스. 활성 상태만 마진을 창출하며, 휴면 상태는 재활성화될 수 있으나 흡수 상태인 이탈 상태로 크게 누출된다."
flowchart LR
  ACT["활성 상태 (Active)<br/>(보상: 100)"]
  LAP["휴면 상태 (Lapsed)<br/>(보상: 0)"]
  LST["이탈 상태 (Lost)<br/>(보상: 0, 흡수 상태)"]
  ACT -->|"0.70"| ACT
  ACT -->|"0.20"| LAP
  ACT -->|"0.10"| LST
  LAP -->|"0.30"| ACT
  LAP -->|"0.40"| LAP
  LAP -->|"0.30"| LST
  LST -->|"1.00"| LST
```

```{r markov-clv}
#| message: false
states <- c("active", "lapsed", "lost")
P <- matrix(c(0.70, 0.20, 0.10,
              0.30, 0.40, 0.30,
              0.00, 0.00, 1.00),
            nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(states, states))
reward <- c(active = 100, lapsed = 0, lost = 0)
gamma  <- 1 / 1.10                                   # 기간당 10% 할인
V <- solve(diag(3) - gamma * P) %*% reward           # 수식 @eq-clv-markov
```

```{r markov-clv-tbl}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-clv-markov
#| tbl-cap: "현재 상태별 마르코프 체인 CLV. 활성 고객은 휴면 고객보다 훨씬 높은 가치를 가짐."
knitr::kable(
  tibble(`현재 상태` = states, `CLV ($)` = round(V[, 1], 2))
)
```

## 머신러닝 및 딥러닝 프런티어 {#sec-clv-ml}

프로덕션의 지배적 패턴은 **2단계 이탈-지출 분해(two-stage churn-times-spend)**이다: 1단계 분류기가 활성 확률을 예측하고, 2단계 회귀모형이 조건부 지출액을 예측한다 [@neslin2006churn].

```{r ml-two-stage}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(glmnet)
library(randomForest)

set.seed(11)
N <- 5000
feat <- tibble(
  recency   = runif(N, 0, 52),
  frequency = rpois(N, 3),
  monetary  = rgamma(N, 4, 0.08),
  tenure    = runif(N, 1, 104),
  promo     = rbinom(N, 1, 0.4))

eta      <- -1 + 0.03 * feat$frequency - 0.02 * feat$recency + 0.4 * feat$promo
active   <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(eta))
spend    <- active * rgamma(N, shape = 3, rate = 3 / (feat$monetary * 0.5))
df_ml    <- feat |> mutate(active = factor(active), spend = spend)

tr <- sample(N, 0.7 * N); te <- setdiff(seq_len(N), tr)

# 1단계: 랜덤 포레스트 활성 분류기
rf <- randomForest(active ~ recency + frequency + monetary + tenure + promo,
                   data = df_ml[tr, ], ntree = 200)
p_active_hat <- predict(rf, df_ml[te, ], type = "prob")[, "1"]

# 2단계: 엘라스틱넷 로그 지출 회귀모형
act_tr <- tr[df_ml$active[tr] == "1"]
xtr <- model.matrix(~ recency + frequency + monetary + tenure + promo,
                    df_ml[act_tr, ])[, -1]
ytr <- log(df_ml$spend[act_tr])
cvfit <- cv.glmnet(xtr, ytr, alpha = 0.5)

xte <- model.matrix(~ recency + frequency + monetary + tenure + promo,
                    df_ml[te, ])[, -1]
resid_var <- as.numeric(var(ytr - predict(cvfit, xtr, s = "lambda.min")))
spend_hat <- exp(as.numeric(predict(cvfit, xte, s = "lambda.min")) + 0.5 * resid_var)

pltv_ml <- p_active_hat * spend_hat * 0.6   # 마진율 60%
cat("2단계 평균 예상 pLTV: $", round(mean(pltv_ml), 2), "\n", sep = "")
cat("실현 마진과의 상관계수:",
    round(cor(pltv_ml, df_ml$spend[te] * 0.6), 3), "\n")
```

로그정규 역변환 시 분산 보정 $\exp(0.5\sigma^2)$이 포함되어야 기대 지출액의 과소평가를 방지할 수 있다.

대안적 통합 접근법은 0점 과다(비구매자)와 두터운 우측 꼬리를 동시에 모델링하는 **영과잉 로그정규(Zero-Inflated Lognormal, ZILN)** 손실 함수다 [@wang2019ziln]. [@fig-clv-ml-heads]는 두 구조를 대비한다.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-clv-ml-heads
%%| fig-cap: "머신러닝 pLTV를 위한 두 가지 프로덕션 아키텍처. 2단계 방식은 활성 분류기와 조건부 지출 회귀모형을 결합하며, ZILN 방식은 0의 스파이크와 두터운 우측 꼬리의 결합 우도를 단일 모델로 학습한다."
flowchart TB
  FT["고객 특징 및 이벤트 이력"]
  subgraph TS["2단계: 이탈 x 지출"]
    C1["1단계 분류기:<br/>기간 내 활성 확률"]
    R1["2단계 회귀모형:<br/>활성 고객의 조건부 지출"]
    PD["곱 x 마진, 할인: pLTV"]
    C1 --> PD
    R1 --> PD
  end
  subgraph ZS["결합 헤드: 영과잉 로그정규(ZILN)"]
    ZH["단일 모델이 이탈 로짓,<br/>로그정규 평균 및 척도를 출력"]
    ZE["결합 우도로 학습:<br/>0의 스파이크 + 두터운 우측 꼬리"]
    ZH --> ZE
  end
  FT --> C1
  FT --> R1
  FT --> ZH
```

```{r ziln}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(21)
M <- 6000
x      <- runif(M, -2, 2)
p_buy  <- plogis(-0.5 + 0.9 * x)
buy    <- rbinom(M, 1, p_buy)
spend2 <- buy * rlnorm(M, meanlog = 3 + 0.5 * x, sdlog = 0.6)

# ZILN 음의 로그우도 함수
ziln_nll <- function(par) {
  p  <- plogis(par[1] + par[2] * x)
  ml <- par[3] + par[4] * x
  s  <- exp(par[5])
  ll <- ifelse(spend2 == 0,
               log1p(-p),
               log(p) + dlnorm(pmax(spend2, 1e-8), ml, s, log = TRUE))
  -sum(ll)
}

fit_ziln <- optim(c(0, 0, 3, 0, log(0.6)), ziln_nll, method = "BFGS")
p_hat  <- plogis(fit_ziln$par[1] + fit_ziln$par[2] * x)
E_buy  <- p_hat * exp((fit_ziln$par[3] + fit_ziln$par[4] * x) +
                        exp(fit_ziln$par[5])^2 / 2)
cat("ZILN 모수 (b0, b1, m0, m1, log-sigma):",
    round(fit_ziln$par, 3), "\n")
cat("ZILN 평균 예측 지출액: $", round(mean(E_buy), 2),
    "  실제 평균: $", round(mean(spend2), 2), "\n", sep = "")
```

시퀀스 모형(RNN, 트랜스포머) [@bauerjannach2021seq2seq], 고객 임베딩 [@chamberlain2017embeddings], 초기 LTV 예측 모형 [@sifa2015games] 등이 프런티어를 확장하고 있다.

## 인과적 및 의사결정 중심 CLV {#sec-clv-causal}

CLV를 예측하는 것과 이에 따라 행동하는 것은 다르다. 대표적인 발견은 **유지 활동의 무용성(retention futility)**이다 [@ascarza2018futility]: 이탈 위험이 가장 높은 고객이 반드시 가장 **설득 가능한(persuadable)** 고객은 아니므로, 단순 예측 이탈률에 유지 예산을 투입하는 것은 낭비가 된다. 올바른 타깃팅 기준은 마케팅 개입의 개별 처치 효과인 **업리프트(uplift)**다.

```{r uplift}
#| message: false
set.seed(3)
M2     <- 8000
risk   <- runif(M2)                       # 이탈 위험
uplift <- rnorm(M2, 0.04, 0.03)           # 개입 처치 효과 (위험과 독립)
margin <- 200

top_quintile <- function(v) v >= quantile(v, 0.8)
gain_risk   <- mean(uplift[top_quintile(risk)])   * margin
gain_uplift <- mean(uplift[top_quintile(uplift)]) * margin

cat(sprintf("상관관계 cor(risk, uplift) = %.3f\n", cor(risk, uplift)))
cat(sprintf("타깃 고객당 방어된 마진: 위험 기반 $%.2f vs 업리프트 기반 $%.2f\n",
            gain_risk, gain_uplift))
```

업리프트 기반 타깃팅은 위험 기반 타깃팅 대비 방어 마진을 2배 이상 높인다 [@simester2020policy; @reinartzthomaskumar2005].

## 인접 구성개념 {#sec-clv-adjacent}

[@tbl-clv-constructs]는 CLV의 인접 구성개념들을 요약한다.

| 구성개념 | 핵심 정의 | 대표 문헌 |
|---|---|---|
| 고객 자산 (CE) | 모든 고객 CLV의 총합; 대차대조표상의 수요 측면 자산 | @rustLemonZeithaml2004 |
| 고객 가치 기반 기업평가 | CE가 기업 가치를 견인; 고성장·적자 기업 평가 가능 | @guptaLehmannStuart2004 |
| CLV 모델링 종합 | 실행 가능한 CLV 정의 및 문헌 종합 | @gupta2006modeling |
| CE와 시가총액 | 집계된 CLV가 주주 가치를 추적함 | @kumarshah2009 |
| CBCV (계약적) | 공시된 고객 지표로부터 상장 구독 기업 가치평가 | @mccarthy2017 |
| CBCV (비계약적) | 공시 데이터에 BTYD 모형을 적용하여 비구독 기업 가치평가 | @mccarthyfader2018 |
| 고객 추천 가치 (CRV) | 타 고객 추천을 통해 고객이 창출하는 가치 | @kumarCRV2010 |
| 고객 인게이지먼트 가치 (CEV) | CLV + CRV + 인플루언서 가치 + 지식 가치 | @kumar2010cev |
| 음(-)의 CLV | 충성 고객이 반드시 수익성 있는 것은 아님 (가치 파괴 고객) | @reinartzkumar2002hbr |
| RFM | BTYD 관점과 일치하는 고전적 스코어링 휴리스틱 | @fader2005rfmclv |
| 이탈 / 유지 예측 | CLV의 예측 기반 기저 | @neslin2006churn |
| 구조적 CLV (CPG) | 브랜드 전환 및 예산 제약 모형 기반 CLV | @sunder2016measuring |

: 고객 평생 가치와 관련된 인접 구성개념들. {#tbl-clv-constructs}

## 고객 추천 가치 (CRV) {#sec-clv-crv}

고객은 구전과 추천 프로그램을 통해 타인을 유입시킴으로써 가치를 창출하며, 이 **고객 추천 가치(CRV)**는 CLV와 실증적으로 구별된다 [@kumarCRV2010].

추천 고객은 두 유형으로 나뉜다: 추천이 없었다면 유입되지 않았을 **유형 1(증분 추천)** 고객과 타 채널을 통해 어차피 유입되었을 **유형 2(비증분 추천)** 고객이다. 유형 1 고객은 순 마진 전체가 추천인에게 귀속되지만, 유형 2 고객은 **절감된 획득 비용**만이 추천 가치로 인정된다:

$$
\text{CRV}_i \;=\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{y=1}^{n_1}
   \frac{A_{ty} - a_{ty} - M_{ty} + \text{ACQ1}_{ty}}{(1+r)^{t}}
   \;+\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{y=n_1+1}^{n_2}
   \frac{\text{ACQ2}_{ty}}{(1+r)^{t}}.
$$ {#eq-crv}

## 단위 경제학과 CLV 현금 흐름 할인 {#sec-clv-unit-econ}

[@tbl-clv-unit-econ]은 획득 채널별 단위 경제학 지표를 요약한다.

```{r unit-econ}
#| message: false
channels <- tribble(
  ~channel,       ~cac, ~m_month, ~churn,
  "Organic",        20,       18,   0.03,
  "Paid Search",    95,       20,   0.06,
  "Social",        140,       16,   0.09,
  "Affiliate",      60,       14,   0.05)

unit <- channels |>
  mutate(ltv        = m_month / churn,
         ltv_cac    = round(ltv / cac, 2),
         payback_mo = round(cac / m_month, 1))
```

```{r unit-econ-tbl}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-clv-unit-econ
#| tbl-cap: "획득 채널별 단위 경제학 지표. 유기적 유입은 매우 효율적인 반면 소셜 채널은 LTV:CAC 비율이 1에 가까워 개선이 필요함."
knitr::kable(
  unit |> transmute(채널 = channel, CAC = cac, `월마진` = m_month,
                    이탈률 = churn, LTV = round(ltv, 0),
                    `LTV:CAC` = ltv_cac, `회수기간(월)` = payback_mo)
)
```

[@fig-clv-nrr]은 NRR 워터폴 차트를 보여준다.

```{r nrr-waterfall}
#| label: fig-clv-nrr
#| fig-cap: "순 매출 유지율(NRR) 워터폴 차트. 기초 MRR에서 이탈과 축소가 발생하지만(GRR 100% 미만), 확장이 이를 상회하여 NRR이 100%를 초과함."
#| message: false
start_mrr   <- 100
churn       <- -5
contraction <- -3
expansion   <- 15
grr <- (start_mrr + churn + contraction) / start_mrr
nrr <- (start_mrr + churn + contraction + expansion) / start_mrr

wf <- tibble(
  step  = factor(c("기초 MRR", "이탈", "축소", "확장", "기말 MRR"),
                 levels = c("기초 MRR", "이탈", "축소",
                            "확장", "기말 MRR")),
  delta = c(start_mrr, churn, contraction, expansion, NA)) |>
  mutate(end   = c(start_mrr, cumsum(delta[1:4])[-1], NA),
         end   = ifelse(step == "기말 MRR", cumsum(delta[1:4]), end),
         start = lag(end, default = 0),
         start = ifelse(step %in% c("기초 MRR", "기말 MRR"), 0, start),
         end   = ifelse(step %in% c("기초 MRR", "기말 MRR"),
                        ifelse(step == "기초 MRR", start_mrr,
                                start_mrr + churn + contraction + expansion), end),
         fill  = case_when(step %in% c("기초 MRR", "기말 MRR") ~ "total",
                            delta >= 0 ~ "gain", TRUE ~ "loss"))

ggplot(wf, aes(step, fill = fill)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = as.numeric(step) - 0.4, xmax = as.numeric(step) + 0.4,
                ymin = pmin(start, end), ymax = pmax(start, end))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(total = "#4e79a7", gain = "#59a14f",
                                loss = "#e15759"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "MRR (천 달러)",
       subtitle = sprintf("GRR = %.0f%%   |   NRR = %.0f%%",
                          100 * grr, 100 * nrr)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

[@tbl-clv-dcf]는 할인율 및 평가 시계에 따른 할인 CLV의 민감도 분석을 보여준다.

```{r dcf-sensitivity}
#| message: false
S_curve <- 0.85^(0:60)   # 월 15% 이탈 유지 곡선
m       <- 100           # 월 마진

grid <- expand_grid(r_annual = c(0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15),
                     N = c(12, 24, 60)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(clv = round(sum(m * S_curve[1:(N + 1)] /
                           (1 + r_annual / 12)^(0:N)), 0)) |>
  ungroup()

frac_beyond_y1 <- 1 - sum(m * S_curve[1:13]) / sum(m * S_curve)
```

```{r dcf-tbl}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-clv-dcf
#| tbl-cap: "연간 할인율 및 평가 시계(N개월)에 따른 할인 CLV ($). 시계의 길이가 할인율보다 더 큰 영향을 미침."
knitr::kable(
  grid |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = N, values_from = clv, names_prefix = "N=") |>
    rename(`연할인율(r)` = r_annual)
)
```

```{r dcf-frac}
cat("12개월 이후에 존재하는 (미할인) 평생 가치 비중: ",
    round(frac_beyond_y1, 3), "\n", sep = "")
```

## 식별과 한계 요인 {#sec-clv-identification}

- **불변 유지율 편향**: 이질적 고객 집단에 불변 $\rho$를 적용하면 장기 고객 가치가 과소평가됨 (sBG 모형으로 해결).
- **시계 및 할인율**: 가치의 상당 부분이 1년 이후에 존재하므로 적절한 $N$과 $r$ 설정이 필수적임.
- **내생적 마케팅 비용**: 마케팅 지출은 가치 있는 고객에게 집중되므로 단순 관찰 상관관계는 인과적 투자 수익률을 왜곡함 (업리프트 모델링 필요).
- **비계약적 환경의 잠재 이탈**: 구매 침묵 고객 중 이탈자와 휴면자를 분리하기 위해 BTYD 모형이 필수적임.
- **생존자 편향 및 데이터 누수**: 엄격한 시점 분할을 통한 데이터 엔지니어링이 요구됨.

## 핵심 요약 {#sec-clv-takeaways}

- CLV([@eq-clv-general])는 고객을 미래지향적 자산(유지 비용을 차감한 미래 마진의 현재가치)으로 다루며, 집계 시 기업 가치를 추적하는 *고객 자산*이 된다.
- 계약적/비계약적 및 이산/연속 분류 체계([@tbl-clv-taxonomy])가 적용 가능한 모형군을 결정한다.
- 단순 공식([@eq-clv-naive])은 잔존 고객 가치를 과소평가하고 이탈률이 0에 가까울 때 발산하며 확장을 무시한다.
- 집계 유지율이 상승하는 것은 개인 충성도 증가가 아닌 *선별(sorting)* 효과 때문이며, sBG 모형([@eq-sbg-survivor])이 이를 포착한다.
- 비계약적 환경에서는 BTYD 모형(Pareto/NBD, BG/NBD)과 Gamma-Gamma 모형이 RFM 데이터로부터 pLTV를 도출한다.
- 머신러닝 pLTV는 2단계 분해 또는 ZILN 손실 함수를 사용하며, 정확도 향상이 실질적 캠페인 이익으로 연결될 때 가치를 갖는다.
- CLV에 기반한 행동은 수준이 아닌 *업리프트*를 목표로 해야 한다 [@ascarza2018futility].


<!-- ====== Section from: 14-celebrity-endorsement.qmd ====== -->

# 유명인 보증 {#sec-celebrity-endorsement}

A *celebrity endorser* is an individual who enjoys public recognition and lends
that recognition to a consumer good by appearing with it in advertising
[@mccracken1989]. Firms spend heavily on this practice because a famous face
appears to do something a product claim cannot: it imports ready-made meaning—
status, competence, glamour, rebelliousness—into a brand that would otherwise
have to manufacture those associations slowly and at great cost. The endorsement
contract is, in effect, the rental of an accumulated reputation. The central
empirical questions are therefore the same ones we ask of any intangible asset:
*through what mechanism does the asset create value, how is that value measured,
and what is the risk that it evaporates?*

This chapter treats celebrity endorsement as a problem with three faces. The
first is **psychological**: why does an endorser change what a consumer thinks
and does? Two classical models—source credibility and source attractiveness—
locate the answer in properties of the *source* (expertise, trust, likability,
similarity). A third, the **meaning-transfer** model, relocates it in *culture*:
the endorser is a conduit that moves symbolic meaning from the culturally
constituted world into the brand and finally into the consumer's own identity
project [@mccracken1986; @mccracken1989]. The second face is **strategic**: which
celebrity should endorse which brand? The *match-up hypothesis* answers that
congruence between endorser and product governs effectiveness, and we give it a
formal, testable structure. The third face is **financial**: endorsement
contracts are firm-level investments whose announcement moves stock prices, whose
returns can be estimated by event study, and whose downside—**endorser risk**—is
the possibility that a scandal contaminates every brand the celebrity touches.

By the end of the chapter the reader should be able to state each model's
construct definitions formally, specify and estimate a match-up interaction,
design an event study that isolates the firm-value effect of an endorsement (and
of an endorser's disgrace), and reason quantitatively about whether an
endorsement is worth its price. Throughout, intuition leads and formalism
follows immediately, in the house manner. Celebrity endorsement is best understood
as a special case of the broader machinery developed in @sec-branding (brands as
networks of meaning and as priced firm assets) and @sec-marketing-finance
(event-study valuation of marketing actions); we draw on both.

## 개념적 토대

The persuasion literature offers two distinct reasons a message recipient might
be moved by *who* delivers a message rather than *what* the message says. The
distinction matters because the two routes have different boundary conditions and
different vulnerabilities, and because the dominant modern model—meaning
transfer—rejects both as incomplete.

### 정보원 신뢰성 모형

The **source credibility** model holds that a communicator's persuasiveness rises
with the audience's perception that the source both *knows* the truth and is
*willing to tell it*. Following the formalization that @mccracken1989 inherits
from the Hovland tradition, credibility has two components. **Expertise** (or
expertness) is the perceived ability of the source to make valid assertions—the
degree to which the endorser is seen as a legitimate source of knowledge about
the product class. **Trustworthiness** is the perceived willingness of the source
to make valid assertions—the audience's confidence that the endorser is reporting
honestly rather than shilling. A message is most effective when the source scores
high on both: a credentialed dermatologist endorsing a skin cream is persuasive
to the extent the audience believes she knows skin *and* is not merely paid to
say so.

> An endorser is effective to the extent the audience perceives the source as
> able to make valid assertions (expertise) and willing to make them
> (trustworthiness); credibility is the conjunction of the two.
> — after the source-credibility tradition synthesized in @mccracken1989

The model's empirical workhorse is the **Ohanian source scale**, which
operationalizes expertise, trustworthiness, and attractiveness as reflective
multi-item semantic-differential batteries.[^ohanian] Its appeal is that it
yields a clean mediation story: endorser characteristics raise perceived
credibility, which raises attitude toward the ad ($A_{ad}$), which raises
attitude toward the brand ($A_b$) and purchase intention. Its limitation, which
motivated the meaning-transfer turn, is that credibility ratings poorly predict
why a *non-expert* celebrity—an actor with no plausible product knowledge—can
nonetheless sell cars, watches, and soft drinks.

[^ohanian]: The 15-item credibility scale (attractiveness, trustworthiness,
expertise) is the field's most-used instrument; we describe its structure rather
than reproduce it, since the items are reflective indicators of three latent
factors and the construct logic is what matters here. <!-- CITE-NEEDED: Ohanian (1990) source credibility scale, JoA -->

### 정보원 매력도 모형

The **source attractiveness** model locates persuasion not in epistemic
authority but in the audience's *affinity* for the source. It decomposes
attractiveness into three perceived properties [@mccracken1989]. **Familiarity**
is knowledge of the source through exposure—the sheer accumulated awareness that
makes a face feel known. **Likability** is affection for the source arising from
physical appearance and behavior. **Similarity** is a supposed resemblance
between source and receiver. The model predicts that liked, familiar, and
similar sources persuade more, operating through identification: the receiver
accepts influence because doing so sustains a satisfying self-defining
relationship with the source.

The attractiveness model rationalizes the use of physically beautiful endorsers
and explains a robust laboratory regularity—attractive sources lift ad and brand
attitudes—but it shares the credibility model's defect. Treating attractiveness
as a *generic* positive trait predicts that the most beautiful celebrity should
sell everything equally well, which is false: an Olympic sprinter sells running
shoes better than perfume, and a supermodel the reverse. The data demand a model
in which the *content* of the celebrity's image, not merely its valence,
determines what the celebrity can sell. That is the contribution of meaning
transfer.

### 의미 이전 모형

@mccracken1989 argues that both classical models are too thin: they reduce a
culturally rich figure to a few scalar traits and cannot explain
*image-specific* effectiveness. The **meaning-transfer** model replaces source
*properties* with the *symbolic meanings* a celebrity carries—status, class,
gender, age, personality, and lifestyle—accumulated across the roles, contexts,
and performances in which the public has encountered the person. The celebrity is
valuable precisely because these meanings are sharply drawn and already
established in the audience's mind.

Meaning moves in three stages, sketched in @fig-meaning-transfer. In the first
stage, cultural meaning resides in the **culturally constituted world** and
becomes attached to celebrities through their public lives. In the second,
**advertising** transfers a selected subset of that meaning from celebrity to
**product**: the ad's creative task is to make the audience see the same meanings
in the brand that they already see in the endorser. In the third, **consumption
rituals** transfer meaning from the product to the **consumer**, who acquires and
displays the good to construct and signal an identity. This third stage rests on
the same premise as the rest of @sec-branding—that consumers consume to build the
*extended self* [@belk1988]—and is enacted through the possession, exchange,
grooming, and divestment rituals through which the broader cultural system moves
meaning into goods [@mccracken1986].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-meaning-transfer
%%| fig-cap: "The meaning-transfer model. Cultural meaning flows from the constituted world to the celebrity, from the celebrity to the brand via advertising, and from the brand to the consumer via consumption rituals. Each arrow is a transfer the marketer must actively engineer; meaning does not move on its own."
flowchart LR
  A["Culturally<br/>constituted world<br/><i>(status, class, gender,<br/>lifestyle)</i>"] -->|public roles<br/>& performances| B["Celebrity<br/>endorser"]
  B -->|advertising| C["Brand /<br/>product"]
  C -->|consumption<br/>rituals| D["Consumer's<br/>extended self"]
  classDef world fill:#eef,stroke:#557;
  classDef person fill:#efe,stroke:#575;
  class A world;
  class D person;
```

Four **modes of endorsement** govern how explicitly the celebrity is bound to the
product within the ad, and thus how directly meaning is invited to transfer
[@mccracken1989]. In the **explicit** mode the endorser states "I endorse this
product"; in the **implicit** mode, "I use this product"; in the **imperative**
mode, "you should use this product"; and in the **copresent** mode the celebrity
merely appears alongside the product, asserting nothing. The copresent mode is the
purest meaning-transfer device—no claim is made, yet the juxtaposition licenses
the audience to read the celebrity's meanings into the brand—and it is precisely
the mode the credibility and attractiveness models cannot explain, because no
assertion is made whose validity expertise or trust could underwrite.

The three models are best read as nested in explanatory ambition rather than as
rivals, as @tbl-three-models summarizes. Credibility and attractiveness identify
*which source traits* matter; meaning transfer explains *why a given trait matters
for a given brand* and supplies the bridge to the match-up hypothesis below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-three-models
#| tbl-cap: "Three models of endorser influence. Each row states the locus of persuasion, the primitive constructs, the mechanism, and the empirical anomaly that the next model down was built to resolve."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr)
m <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Source credibility", "Source attractiveness", "Meaning transfer"),
  `Locus of persuasion` = c("Epistemic authority of the source",
                            "Audience affinity for the source",
                            "Cultural meanings the source carries"),
  `Primitive constructs` = c("Expertise; trustworthiness",
                            "Familiarity; likability; similarity",
                            "Status, class, gender, age, lifestyle"),
  `Unresolved anomaly` = c("Non-expert celebrities still sell",
                         "Beauty does not sell all categories equally",
                         "Requires congruence logic (match-up)"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(m)
```

## 적합성 가설

If a celebrity's value is the *specific* meaning she carries, then effectiveness
must depend on the *fit* between that meaning and the brand. The **match-up
hypothesis** states exactly this: an endorser is more effective the more
congruent the endorser's image is with the endorsed product. The hypothesis is
the strategic operationalization of meaning transfer—it tells the manager not
merely to hire a credible or attractive celebrity but to hire one whose
accumulated meanings *match* the meanings the brand wishes to own.

### 직관과 형식화

The intuition is a congruence-as-interaction claim: endorser quality and brand
relevance are complements, not substitutes. A high-meaning endorser adds little
to a brand the meaning does not fit, and a perfectly matched but low-profile
endorser has little meaning to transfer. Let $y$ denote a response outcome
(attitude toward the brand, purchase intention, or choice). Let $E$ index a
property of the endorser (e.g., perceived attractiveness or expertise, mean-
centered) and let $M$ denote the *match*—the congruence between the endorser's
image and the product category, also mean-centered. The match-up hypothesis is
the claim that the two interact:

$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 E + \beta_2 M + \beta_3\,(E \times M) + \varepsilon,
\qquad H_{\text{match-up}}:\ \beta_3 > 0.
$$ {#eq-matchup}

The substantive content is entirely in $\beta_3$. A positive interaction means
the marginal effect of endorser quality, $\partial y / \partial E = \beta_1 +
\beta_3 M$, *grows* with match: the same attractive celebrity moves the outcome
more for a beauty product than for a power tool. The main effects $\beta_1$ and
$\beta_2$ are, on the match-up logic, of secondary interest; a model that omits
the product term and reports only that "attractive endorsers work" has not tested
the hypothesis at all. This is the same interaction-versus-main-effect distinction
that governs brand-extension fit in @sec-branding, and it carries the same warning:
congruence is a *relational* property and must be modeled relationally.

### 재현 가능한 검정

Identification of $\beta_3$ in an experiment is clean because $E$ and $M$ are
*assigned*, not measured: a $2 \times 2$ design crosses a high- versus low-
attractiveness endorser with a high- versus low-match product, and randomization
guarantees the regressors are orthogonal to $\varepsilon$, so least squares
recovers the interaction without confounding. The estimator is ordinary least
squares (OLS); the identifying assumption is random assignment of the endorser–
product pairing (which makes $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid E, M] = 0$); and what
breaks identification in *observational* endorsement data is that firms *choose*
matched endorsers, so $M$ correlates with unobserved brand quality and $\beta_3$
absorbs selection. The simulation below generates data under @eq-matchup with a
known positive interaction and recovers it.

```{r}
#| label: matchup-sim
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(1989)  # year of McCracken's meaning-transfer paper

n_per_cell <- 60
design <- expand.grid(
  endorser = c(-0.5, 0.5),   # low / high attractiveness (effect-coded)
  match    = c(-0.5, 0.5),   # low / high product match
  rep      = seq_len(n_per_cell)
)

# True data-generating process: positive match-up interaction (beta_3 = 1.4)
b0 <- 3.0; b1 <- 0.4; b2 <- 0.6; b3 <- 1.4
design$y <- with(design,
  b0 + b1 * endorser + b2 * match + b3 * (endorser * match) +
    rnorm(nrow(design), sd = 1))

fit <- lm(y ~ endorser * match, data = design)
round(summary(fit)$coefficients, 3)

# Cell means make the interaction visible: the endorser "lift" is large only
# when the product matches.
cell <- aggregate(y ~ endorser + match, data = design, FUN = mean)
lift_match    <- with(cell, y[endorser == 0.5 & match == 0.5] -
                              y[endorser == -0.5 & match == 0.5])
lift_mismatch <- with(cell, y[endorser == 0.5 & match == -0.5] -
                              y[endorser == -0.5 & match == -0.5])
cat("Endorser lift when matched:    ", round(lift_match, 2), "\n")
cat("Endorser lift when mismatched: ", round(lift_mismatch, 2), "\n")
```

The estimated `endorser:match` coefficient recovers the planted $\beta_3$, and the
two "lift" quantities make the substantive claim concrete: switching to the
attractive endorser helps far more when the product matches than when it does not.
A non-significant interaction—not a significant main effect—is what would falsify
the hypothesis.

### 범위, 메커니즘, 경계

The match-up effect is not unconditional, and the modern literature has mapped its
boundaries. The processing route matters: under the elaboration-likelihood logic
of @petty1983 and @petty1986, source cues such as attractiveness operate as
*peripheral* cues when involvement is low and the audience is not scrutinizing
arguments, but as substantive evidence (or as a distraction) when involvement is
high. Congruence therefore interacts with involvement, and an endorser who helps a
low-involvement impulse purchase may be irrelevant or counterproductive for a
high-involvement considered one. The mechanism also runs partly through *transfer
of affect*: positive feelings conditioned to the celebrity can become attached to
the brand through co-occurrence, a classical-conditioning account that complements
meaning transfer and that, like it, predicts congruence-dependent effects rather
than uniform lift. Finally, the **multiple-product / multiple-endorser** problem
complicates the simple match-up story: a celebrity who endorses many unrelated
brands dilutes the distinctiveness of the meaning available for transfer to any
one of them, weakening congruence even when each pairing is individually
well matched. <!-- CITE-NEEDED: Tripp, Jensen & Carlson (1994) multiple-product endorsement dilution, JCR -->

Two cross-cultural moderators deserve emphasis because they bound external
validity. Power-distance belief—the extent to which a consumer accepts hierarchy—
moderates the celebrity effect: power-distance beliefs *strengthen* the positive
effect of celebrity (versus non-celebrity) endorsers on advertising evaluations,
because celebrities are high-status sources whose influence is more readily
accepted by those who endorse hierarchical social arrangements [@Winterich_2018].
This is a meaning-transfer result in disguise—status is one of the cultural
meanings a celebrity carries, and its persuasive force depends on whether the
audience values status. Self-construal further conditions which connection
matters, paralleling the brand-attachment findings of @swaminathan2007.

## 보증인으로서의 인플루언서

The economics of endorsement have been reshaped by social-media **influencers**—
individuals who accumulate audiences on platforms and monetize that attention
through paid brand content. Influencers occupy an intermediate position between
the classical celebrity and the ordinary peer: they are more *similar* to their
followers than a film star (raising the attractiveness model's similarity lever)
yet command genuine reach, and their persuasiveness depends sharply on perceived
authenticity. @sokolova2020 show that parasocial interaction and the perceived
credibility of the influencer drive purchase intention, with engagement operating
through identification rather than expertise. Disclosure of the commercial
relationship is the new trust frontier: sponsorship transparency interacts with
follower trust in ways the original trustworthiness construct anticipated but
could not have specified. Influencer marketing is now an industry of its own, with
intermediaries matching brands to creators [@nistor2024influencers], and even
*mega*-influencer and celebrity-creator effects have been documented in
firm-outcome data [@tian2024mega; @leung2022]. The constructs are old; the
measurement environment—observable, high-frequency, and platform-mediated—is new.

## 보증인 위험

The asset a firm rents in an endorsement is a *person*, and persons misbehave. The
defining hazard of celebrity endorsement is therefore **endorser risk**: the brand
inherits not only the celebrity's favorable meanings but also her liabilities, and
a scandal can transfer *negative* meaning into the brand through exactly the
channel of @fig-meaning-transfer that was supposed to transfer positive meaning. A
serious treatment of endorsement must price this downside, not merely the upside.

Several features make endorser risk distinctive. It is *idiosyncratic to the
person* and largely outside the firm's control, so it cannot be diversified within
a single endorsement. It is *transferable*: meaning transfer is symmetric, and the
same congruence that amplifies positive transfer amplifies the contamination when
the endorser's image sours. And it is *correlated across a celebrity's
portfolio*—one scandal simultaneously damages every brand the celebrity endorses,
which is why endorsement contracts contain morality clauses permitting termination
on disrepute. The negative information need not even be deserved: under the
attribution logic that governs brand crises in @sec-branding, audiences who view
character as stable (entity theorists) generalize a transgression to a global
judgment of the person, and that judgment flows to the brand.

The timing of harm is subtle. A *sleeper effect* can arise when a discounting
cue—"this source is untrustworthy"—decays faster than the message itself, so
persuasion *rises* over time as the audience forgets why it discounted the
source; symmetrically, the damage from a tainted endorser can dissipate as the
association weakens, so the net effect of a scandal is dynamic rather than a
one-time level shift [@wu2015sleeping]. Managers who read a scandal's immediate
stock-price reaction as the whole story may therefore mis-estimate the long-run
cost, in either direction.

## 보증과 기업가치

Endorsement contracts are firm-level investments, and capital markets price them.
The natural identification strategy is the **event study** developed in
@sec-marketing-finance: an endorsement announcement (or an endorser scandal) is a
discrete, dated event whose firm-value consequence is read from the abnormal
stock return in a tight window around the announcement, after the normal return is
removed.

### 사건연구 추정량

For firm $i$ on trading day $t$, the **abnormal return** is the realized return
minus its expectation under a market model estimated on a clean pre-event window:

$$
\mathrm{AR}_{it} = R_{it} - \big(\hat\alpha_i + \hat\beta_i R_{mt}\big),
\qquad
\mathrm{CAR}_i(W) = \sum_{t \in W} \mathrm{AR}_{it},
$$ {#eq-car}

where $R_{mt}$ is the market return, $(\hat\alpha_i, \hat\beta_i)$ are OLS
estimates from the estimation window, and $\mathrm{CAR}_i(W)$ is the cumulative
abnormal return over a short event window $W$ (often $[-1, +1]$ days). The method
is the standard apparatus of @mcwilliams1997a and @srinivasan2004event and is
applied to brand-asset transactions in @sec-branding.

Three assumptions carry the inference, and each is a place identification can
break. **Market efficiency**: prices impound the news quickly, so a short window
captures the full effect; if the news leaks, the window must widen and power
falls. **No confounding**: the window must be scrubbed of contemporaneous
firm-specific news—earnings, splits, executive changes, buybacks, dividend
changes—because the event study cannot separate two events sharing a window
[@srinivasan2004event]. **Correct normal-return model**: a misspecified benchmark
($\hat\alpha, \hat\beta$) contaminates every $\mathrm{AR}$; thin trading and
event-induced variance further bias the standard errors. The estimator answers a
sharp question—*by how much did this announcement change shareholder wealth?*—only
to the extent these assumptions hold.

### 재현 가능한 사건연구

The following example simulates daily returns for a firm, injects a positive
endorsement-announcement effect on the event day, estimates the market model on
the pre-event window, and aggregates abnormal returns over a three-day event
window. The structure mirrors exactly what one would run on CRSP data.

```{r}
#| label: event-study-sim
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(2024)

est_days   <- 120          # estimation window length
event_win  <- -1:1         # 3-day event window around the announcement
n_days     <- est_days + length(event_win)

# True market model: R_it = alpha + beta * R_mt + e_it, with a +1.8% jump on day 0
alpha <- 0.0002; beta <- 1.1; sigma <- 0.012
r_m   <- rnorm(n_days, mean = 0.0004, sd = 0.009)
shock <- rep(0, n_days); shock[est_days + which(event_win == 0)] <- 0.018
r_i   <- alpha + beta * r_m + shock + rnorm(n_days, sd = sigma)

# Estimate the market model on the clean pre-event window only
est_idx <- seq_len(est_days)
mm  <- lm(r_i[est_idx] ~ r_m[est_idx])
ab  <- coef(mm)[1]; bt <- coef(mm)[2]

# Abnormal returns over the event window
ev_idx <- (est_days + 1):n_days
AR  <- r_i[ev_idx] - (ab + bt * r_m[ev_idx])
CAR <- sum(AR)

# Test statistic: CAR scaled by the estimation-window residual SD
sd_ar  <- sd(residuals(mm))
t_stat <- CAR / (sd_ar * sqrt(length(ev_idx)))

cat("Estimated alpha, beta:", round(ab, 5), round(bt, 3), "\n")
cat("Daily abnormal returns:", paste(round(AR, 4), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("CAR over [-1,+1]:      ", round(CAR, 4),
    sprintf("(%.2f%%)", 100 * CAR), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:           ", round(t_stat, 2), "\n")
```

The recovered $\mathrm{CAR}$ concentrates on the event day and is statistically
distinguishable from zero, reproducing the planted announcement effect. An
endorser-scandal study is the same machinery with the sign reversed and the event
redefined as the disclosure date.

### 증거가 보여 주는 것

Applied work using this design finds that endorsement is, on average, value
creating but heavily conditional. Announcements of celebrity-endorsement contracts
are associated with positive abnormal returns and with gains in sales, and the
effect is larger when the endorser is well matched and athletically or
reputationally distinguished [@agrawal2000; @elberse2003]. Athlete endorsements in
particular raise the sponsoring firm's sales and stock returns, with the lift
tracking the athlete's on-field success and visibility [@elberse2003]. The downside
is equally real and is priced: negative information about an endorser—arrest,
scandal, doping—transfers to the brand and to firm value, and the contamination is
stronger where the celebrity–brand link is tighter, the mirror image of the
match-up amplification [@chuluun2017firm]. Endorsement, like co-branding in
@sec-branding, is thus a *reputation-coupling* decision: the firm gains access to
the celebrity's reputational capital but assumes a share of its variance.

@tbl-endorser-risk frames the trade-off as a simple expected-value problem and
foreshadows the quantitative reasoning a manager should bring to a contract.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-endorser-risk
#| tbl-cap: "Endorsement as a risky investment. The expected firm-value effect nets the probability-weighted upside of a well-received campaign against the probability-weighted downside of an endorser scandal, minus the contract's cost. A high-match endorser raises both the upside and the contamination severity."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr)
risk <- data.frame(
  Component = c("Upside (successful campaign)",
                "Downside (endorser scandal)",
                "Contract cost",
                "Net expected value"),
  `Driver` = c("Match x reach x meaning fit",
             "Scandal probability x contamination severity",
             "Negotiated fee + activation spend",
             "E[upside] - E[downside] - cost"),
  `Match-up role` = c("Raises upside (amplifies positive transfer)",
                    "Raises severity (amplifies negative transfer)",
                    "Higher for higher-meaning endorsers",
                    "Match-up enters with opposite signs"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(risk)
```

### 개략적 가치평가

The table's logic is worth making numerical, because it disciplines the romance of
a marquee signing. Treat the endorsement as a one-period lottery: with probability
$1-q$ the campaign succeeds and adds value $V^{+}$; with probability $q$ a scandal
strikes and subtracts $V^{-}$; the contract costs $C$. The endorsement is
ex-ante value creating only if

$$
(1-q)\,V^{+} \;-\; q\,V^{-} \;-\; C \;>\; 0.
$$ {#eq-endorser-ev}

Match-up enters @eq-endorser-ev with *opposite signs* on $V^{+}$ and $V^{-}$: a
tighter celebrity–brand coupling raises the success payoff $V^{+}$ but also raises
the contamination loss $V^{-}$, so the optimal match is interior, not maximal,
once risk is priced. The snippet below evaluates the criterion and the breakeven
scandal probability.

```{r}
#| label: endorser-ev
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
V_up   <- 40e6     # firm-value gain if the campaign succeeds
V_down <- 120e6    # firm-value loss if the endorser is disgraced
C      <- 15e6     # contract + activation cost
q      <- 0.05     # annual scandal probability

ev <- (1 - q) * V_up - q * V_down - C
q_breakeven <- (V_up - C) / (V_up + V_down)

cat("Expected value of the endorsement: $",
    format(round(ev), big.mark = ","), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Breakeven scandal probability:     ",
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * q_breakeven), "\n")
```

The breakeven probability—the scandal rate at which the endorsement is exactly
worth its cost—falls as the contamination loss $V^{-}$ rises, which is why brands
with the most to lose (those whose match is tightest and whose equity is largest)
are the most sensitive to endorser conduct and the most aggressive about morality
clauses. The model is deliberately spare, but it captures the governing tension:
the very congruence the match-up hypothesis prescribes is also what makes a
scandal expensive.

## 함정과 식별

The recurring threat in endorsement research is **selection**. Firms do not pair
celebrities with brands at random; they hire matched, attractive, credible
endorsers precisely for valuable brands and well-funded campaigns. In
observational data the match variable $M$ in @eq-matchup is therefore correlated
with unobserved brand quality and campaign budget, so a naive regression overstates
the causal effect of congruence and the event-study $\mathrm{CAR}$ in @eq-car
blends the endorsement's effect with the information the announcement reveals about
the firm's prospects. Experiments solve this by assigning the pairing; event
studies mitigate it by differencing against the market and scrubbing confounds, but
neither fully removes the firm's *choice* of when and whom to announce.

A second pitfall is **construct conflation**. Credibility, attractiveness, and
meaning are distinct, and a study that measures only generic "endorser
favorability" cannot adjudicate among the three models or test the match-up
interaction, which requires a *product-relative* match measure. A third is
**dynamics**: the sleeper effect [@wu2015sleeping] and the gradual decay of
meaning mean that a single post-event snapshot can mislead; effects should be
traced over a horizon. A fourth, specific to influencers, is **disclosure
endogeneity**: sponsored posts are selectively disclosed and selectively
produced, so the apparent effect of an influencer confounds the creator's choice
of which products to promote with the persuasion itself [@nistor2024influencers].
Each pitfall is an instance of the general principle that runs through this book—
state the assignment mechanism before interpreting the estimate.

## 핵심 요점

- A celebrity endorser rents an accumulated reputation; the three classical
  models locate its persuasive force in *credibility* (expertise, trust),
  *attractiveness* (familiarity, likability, similarity), and—most completely—
  *meaning transfer* of specific cultural meanings from celebrity to brand to
  consumer [@mccracken1986; @mccracken1989].
- The **match-up hypothesis** is the testable, interaction-based ($\beta_3 > 0$
  in @eq-matchup) operationalization of meaning transfer; a significant main
  effect without a significant interaction does not test it.
- Endorser influence is moderated by processing route [@petty1986], cultural
  values such as power distance [@Winterich_2018], and—for influencers—perceived
  authenticity and disclosure [@sokolova2020].
- **Endorser risk** is the symmetric, transferable, portfolio-correlated downside
  of meaning transfer; tighter match amplifies *both* the upside and the
  contamination, so the value-maximizing match is interior once risk is priced
  (@eq-endorser-ev).
- Endorsement contracts and scandals are firm-level events whose value effect is
  estimated by **event study** (@eq-car); the evidence shows positive average
  returns to well-matched, high-reputation endorsements and significant losses to
  endorser scandals [@agrawal2000; @elberse2003; @chuluun2017firm], subject
  always to the selection caveat that firms choose whom, and when, to announce.
